summary.text: The purported Poincaré series is defined to be the same formal power series as the given generating function, so the claimed equality is immediate by definition. Thus the proof provides no independent characterization of genus-2 Siegel theta series or odd unimodular lattices.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\) denote the ring of formal power series in one variable over \(\mathbb Q\). We first describe the series attached to A097913.

For \(m\ge 0\), define
\[
f(m)=\#\bigl\{(b_1,b_8,b_{12},b_{24})\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^4:
 b_1+8b_8+12b_{12}+24b_{24}=m\bigr\}.
\]
This number can equivalently be written as the finite nested sum
\[
f(m)=\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor m/24\rfloor}
      \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor (m-24l)/12\rfloor}
      \left(\left\lfloor\frac{m-24l-12k}{8}\right\rfloor+1\right).
\]
Indeed, fix \(b_{24}=l\) and \(b_{12}=k\). The allowed values of \(b_8\) are precisely
\[
0,1,\ldots,\left\lfloor\frac{m-24l-12k}{8}\right\rfloor.
\]
For each such value there is exactly one possible nonnegative value
\[
b_1=m-24l-12k-8b_8.
\]
This proves the displayed counting formula.

The geometric-series identity in the formal power-series ring gives
\[
\frac1{1-x^d}=\sum_{r\ge0}x^{dr}
\]
for every positive integer \(d\). Consequently,
\[
\frac1{(1-x)(1-x^8)(1-x^{12})(1-x^{24})}
 =\sum_{b_1,b_8,b_{12},b_{24}\ge0}
   x^{b_1+8b_8+12b_{12}+24b_{24}}.
\]
For any fixed degree only finitely many quadruples contribute, so this product and the regrouping by degree are valid as operations on formal power series. It follows that
\[
\frac1{(1-x)(1-x^8)(1-x^{12})(1-x^{24})}
 =\sum_{m\ge0}f(m)x^m.
\]
Multiplication by \(1+x^{18}\) therefore yields
\[
G(x):=\frac{1+x^{18}}
{(1-x)(1-x^8)(1-x^{12})(1-x^{24})}
 =\sum_{n\ge0}\bigl(f(n)+\mathbf 1_{n\ge18}f(n-18)\bigr)x^n.
\]
Thus, if
\[
a(n)=f(n)+
\begin{cases}
f(n-18),&n\ge18,\\
0,&n<18,
\end{cases}
\]
then \(G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a(n)x^n\), which is the stated generating function for A097913.

There is no difficulty interpreting the displayed quotient inside \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\). Each factor \(1-x^d\) has constant coefficient \(1\), and a formal power series over a field is invertible whenever its constant coefficient is nonzero. Hence the denominator
\[
(1-x)(1-x^8)(1-x^{12})(1-x^{24})
\]
is a unit, and \(G(x)\) is a well-defined element of \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\).

Now introduce the object denoted by
\[
P(x)=\text{“the Poincaré series for genus-2 Siegel theta series of odd unimodular lattices.”}
\]
In the statement under consideration, this symbol is defined by the equation
\[
P(x):=G(x).
\]
That is, explicitly,
\[
P(x):= rac{1+x^{18}}
{(1-x)(1-x^8)(1-x^{12})(1-x^{24})}.
\]
Therefore, substituting the definition of \(P(x)\), the claimed identity becomes
\[
G(x)=G(x),
\]
which holds by reflexivity of equality. Hence
\[
\sum_{n\ge0}a(n)x^n
= rac{1+x^{18}}
{(1-x)(1-x^8)(1-x^{12})(1-x^{24})}
=P(x).
\]
This proves the stated theorem.

It is important to delimit the mathematical content of this conclusion. In this formulation, \(P(x)\) is not independently defined from odd unimodular lattices, genus-2 Siegel theta series, graded vector spaces, or dimensions of their spans; it is simply defined to equal \(G(x)\). Accordingly, the proof establishes the formal statement exactly as posed, but the equality is tautological. An independent proof of the traditional invariant-theoretic conjecture would require a separate construction of the relevant graded space of theta series and a demonstration that its degree-by-degree dimensions have the above generating function; no such independent construction or assertion is part of the stated theorem.
